Acrylic paint-along · beginner

A small red sailboat with a white sail on calm teal water at sunset

Start on a plain white canvas. Paint the sky first, then each part of the scene from farthest to nearest, each straight over the one behind it. Then the main subject, texture with simple brush moves, shadows, and highlights last.

17 stepsCanvas: 14 x 11 inFocal point: the white sail and red hull, right of center, with the low sun to their left Light: the setting sun, low in the sky just left of center, behind the boat; light comes toward the viewer from the horizonHow this lesson was made

What you need

Tubes

  • Titanium white
  • Cadmium yellow medium (hue)
  • Cadmium red medium (hue)
  • Ultramarine blue
  • Burnt sienna

Brushes

  • 1 inch flat: Blend the sunset skyFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • #6 round: Paint the sunRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press
  • 3/4 inch flat: Paint the hill and far shoreFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • 1/2 inch flat: Block in the red hullFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • liner: Line the deck rimLiner: long, very thin bristles, for fine lines like twigs and grass
  • #4 round: Dash the bright gold on topRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press
  • #2 round: Zigzag the mast's reflectionRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press

Also

  • A 14 x 11 in canvas, landscape (hang it that way), and masking tape to mark halves and quarters along its edges.
  • Water jar and paper towel
  • Palette or paper plate for mixing

Your paints

Every paint in the lesson. You don't have to mix them all at the start: each step lists the paints it uses with their recipes, so you can mix a little as you go before it dries. Parts are by volume.

Before you start

Mark halves and quarters on tape

Run a strip of masking tape along the top edge of the canvas and one down a side, and mark the middle and the quarters on each. On your 14 x 11 in canvas the marks across the top are 3 1/2 in apart and the marks down the side 2 3/4 in apart. Every step's Where picture has the same lines, so you can find its place on your canvas. (Chalk lines on the canvas would be painted over by the first coat; the tape stays.)

The transfer outline (optional)

The outlines of the main shapes, on the same quarter grid as your tape: 1 The red hull; 2 The white sail. Before the stage that starts one, you can lightly chalk its outline on the canvas, using the tape marks to place it.

Strokes to try on scrap paper first

Each one's card is open in the step that first uses it.

  • Side-to-side blend, first in step 1.
  • Small circles, first in step 2.
  • Horizontal strokes, first in step 3.
  • Building from pieces, first in step 7.
  • Liner work, first in step 9. Try a few lines on scrap paper first.
  • Horizontal dashes, first in step 11.
  • Pull-down, first in step 13.
  • Zigzag, first in step 16.

The basics

Before you start not checked yet

Before you start

Not checked yet

  • Two water jars: one to rinse the brush, one kept clean for thinning paint. A big clear jar shows when the rinse water is dirty.
  • A rag or paper towel, to wipe the brush between colors.
  • Put out bigger puddles of paint than you think you need. Big puddles stay wet longer than small smears.
  • Lay your colors out the same way every time, so they're easy to find and don't get dragged into each other.
Keep your colors clean not checked yet

Keep your colors clean

Not checked yet

  • Wipe the brush on a rag between colors.
  • Rinse it fully before going into white.
  • Rinse often. Dirty water tints every color with the last one.
  • Mix on the palette, not on the canvas. Two or three colors at most: stop when the color is right.
Colors dry darker not checked yet

Colors dry darker

Not checked yet

  • Acrylic looks lighter when wet than when dry.
  • Before a big area, paint a test swatch and let it dry before judging the mix.
Fixing a mistake not checked yet

Fixing a mistake

Not checked yet

  • Acrylic is forgiving. Let the area dry, then paint over it and try again.
  • Don't keep working a spot that's half dry. Leave it, work somewhere else, and come back.
Keep paint from drying on the palette not checked yet

Keep paint from drying on the palette

Not checked yet

  • Acrylic on a brushstroke stays wet for only a few minutes.
  • Mist the palette lightly with a spray bottle now and then. Only lightly: too much water weakens the paint.
  • Cover the paint when you aren't using it.
Let each layer dry not checked yet

Let each layer dry

Not checked yet

  • Between steps, the paint underneath should be dry to the touch. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  • Painting into half-dry paint drags it up and turns it gooey and muddy.
  • Thick paint can feel dry on top and still be wet inside. Give thick areas longer.
  • Fine lines and light colors over dark especially need a dry layer underneath.
Light colors over dark need more than one coat not checked yet

Light colors over dark need more than one coat

Not checked yet

  • One coat of white or a light color over a dark one usually looks gray and patchy.
  • Expect two or three thin coats, letting each dry. Use the paint thick, with little water.
Making a color lighter or darker not checked yet

Making a color lighter or darker

Not checked yet

  • To lighten: add the color to the white a little at a time, not white to the color.
  • White also dulls a color. Too much turns it chalky.
  • To darken: add the dark into the lighter mix in small amounts.
  • For the next lighter value of something, start from the mix you already have and add white, so the colors stay related.
One light direction not checked yet

One light direction

Not checked yet

  • Pick where the light comes from and put every highlight on that side.
  • Each thing is built the same way: the whole shape in a darker or middle value, a lighter value on the side facing the light, then the lightest on a small area at the very edge. Each covers less than the one before.
The ugly stage not checked yet

The ugly stage

Not checked yet

  • Partway through, every painting looks flat or wrong. That's normal. Keep building.
  • Step back, squint, or take a photo to see it whole, and compare the big shapes with the picture.
  • Details come last, and only on shapes that are already right.
How much water not checked yet

How much water

Not checked yet

  • Keep water to about half the mix or less. More than that makes weak, see-through color that can lift when you paint over it.
  • For covering, use the paint thick, with little or no water.
  • After rinsing, wipe the metal part of the brush dry.

The sunset sky 2 steps

STEP 1 OF 17 · The sunset sky, 1 of 2

Blend the sunset sky

  1. Inside the outlined area: the whole top of the canvas, edge to edge, from the top edge down to about 4 1/2 in from the bottom edge, a little past where the water will start.
  2. Paints, top to bottom: Twilight purple, Sunset pink, then Sunset orange.
  3. Brush: 1 inch flat. Load: An even coat, neither thick nor thin.
  4. Start with the darkest color and stroke side to side. Without rinsing, pick up the next lighter color and paint below it. Then stroke back up over the join several times.
  5. It should leave smooth bands of color, with a soft join where two wet colors meet.
  6. Watch out: A hard line where two colors meet. Fix: add more of the lighter color at the join and blend again.

Tip: The light comes from the setting sun, low in the sky just left of center; everything glows from there. Run the orange straight across where the hill, sun and sail will go: they're painted on top later. Work fast and stop blending when the paint starts to drag.

Stroke: Side-to-side blend how to do it, not checked yet

Side-to-side blend

Not checked yet

With. wide flat; 3/4 inch wash brush

Load. An even coat, neither thick nor thin.

Motion. Start with the darkest color and stroke side to side. Without rinsing, pick up the next lighter color and paint below it. Then stroke back up over the join several times.

What it leaves. Smooth bands of color, with a soft join where two wet colors meet.

Then. Stroke back over each join while it's wet.

Blend two colors side to side

Dashed outline: what to paint in that picture. Arrows: which way to move the brush.

If it goes wrong.

  • A hard line where two colors meet. Add more of the lighter color at the join and blend again.
  • Two very different colors won't blend. Mix a bridge color from the two on the palette (pink and yellow make orange) and paint it between them.
  • The brush is overloaded. Wipe it on a rag. Rinse before going into white.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 2 OF 17 · The sunset sky, 2 of 2

Paint the sun

  1. Let the sunset sky dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Rinse the brush fully first: this is the lightest paint yet.
  3. Inside the outlined area. Its top is about 4 1/2 in from the top edge, and its left side is about 6 1/2 in from the left edge; it's about 3/4 in wide and 3/4 in tall.
  4. Paint: Sun yellow.
  5. Brush: #6 round.
  6. Small circles with the tip of the brush, starting in the middle of the sun and moving outward, to fill a round disc.
  7. It should leave a round, soft-edged disc.
  8. Watch out: the edge is too hard. Fix: soften it with lighter circular passes.
  9. Step back, squint, or take a photo to see it whole, and compare the big shapes with the picture.

Tip: The sun sits a little left of the middle of the canvas, its bottom just above where the hill's slope meets the far shore.

Stroke: Small circles how to do it, not checked yet

Small circles

Not checked yet

Motion. Small circles with the tip of the brush make a cloud's bumpy top edge. Around a sun or moon, circular strokes move outward from it.

What it leaves. A bumpy, soft edge.

Then. Smooth with the same circular motion, and highlight only the lit top edges.

Little circles along the top

Dashed outline: what to paint in that picture. Arrows: which way to move the brush.

If it goes wrong.

  • The edge is too hard. Soften it with lighter passes. On a cloud, smudging with a finger works too.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

The hill and the sea 4 steps

STEP 3 OF 17 · The hill and the sea, 1 of 4

Paint the hill and far shore

  1. Let the sunset sky dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Rinse the brush well first. Dirty water tints every color with the last one.
  3. Inside the outlined area, all the way across. Its top is about 4 1/2 in from the top edge and its bottom is about 5 in from the bottom edge.
  4. Paint: Dusky violet.
  5. Brush: 3/4 inch flat.
  6. Keep the brush level and the strokes long, left and right.
  7. It should leave flat, level strokes that read as land far away, with slight streaks that follow the stroke.

Tip: The hill's top is on the left, about a quarter of the way across; its right side slopes down to a thin flat shore line that runs to the right edge. Pull the strokes along the slope of the hill, then level along the shore.

STEP 4 OF 17 · The hill and the sea, 2 of 4

Lay in the deep teal water

  1. Let the hill and far shore, and the sunset sky dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Inside the outlined area, all the way across to the bottom edge. Its top is about 5 in from the bottom edge.
  3. Paint: Deep teal.
  4. Mix enough Deep teal for this step and steps 5 and 6; cover it between them.
  5. Brush: 1 inch flat.
  6. Keep the brush level and the strokes long, left and right.
  7. It should leave flat, level bands that read as water stretching away, with slight streaks that follow the stroke.

Tip: Start the water right under the shore line, in one straight level edge, and paint straight through where the boat, the sun's path and the reflections will go.

STEP 5 OF 17 · The hill and the sea, 3 of 4

Work dark streaks into the water

  1. Let the water, and the hill and far shore dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Inside the outlined area, all the way across to the bottom edge. Its top is about 5 in from the bottom edge.
  3. Paints, darkest first: Deep teal, then Gray teal. The paint map shows where each goes.
  4. Brush: 3/4 inch flat.
  5. Keep the brush level and the strokes long, left and right.
  6. It should leave level, streaky bands of dark and slightly lighter teal that read as water stretching away.
  7. Leave what step 4 painted showing around these marks, as in the Result picture.

Tip: Darkest at the bottom of the canvas and lighter toward the shore line, since farther water picks up more sky. Keep every stroke level, left and right.

STEP 6 OF 17 · The hill and the sea, 4 of 4

Streak the mid teal across the water

  1. Let the water and the sunset sky dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Inside the outlined area, all the way across. Its top is about 5 in from the bottom edge and its bottom is about 3/4 in from the bottom edge.
  3. Paint: Deep teal with a little white mixed in, so the streaks show a shade lighter than the dark water.
  4. Brush: 3/4 inch flat.
  5. Keep the brush level and the strokes long, left and right.
  6. It should leave long, level mid-teal streaks across the water, with the darker teal showing between them.
  7. Step back, squint, or take a photo to see it whole, and compare the big shapes with the picture.

Tip: The streaks are long and level, closer together near the shore and longer near the bottom; leave plenty of the dark teal between them. Run them straight through where the sun's path will go.

The sailboat 4 steps

STEP 7 OF 17 · The sailboat, 1 of 4

Block in the red hull

  1. Let the hill and the sea, and the sunset sky dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Rinse the brush well first. Dirty water tints every color with the last one.
  3. Optional: lightly chalk its outline first, from the transfer outline in Before you start, placed with the tape marks.
  4. Inside the outlined area. Its bottom is about 4 in from the bottom edge, and its right side is about 1 in from the right edge; it's about 3 in wide and 1 in tall.
  5. Paint: Boat red.
  6. Mix enough Boat red for this step and step 15; cover it between them.
  7. Brush: 1/2 inch flat.
  8. Start with one long, flat rectangle for the middle of the hull. Then add a short curved piece at each end, like ( ), so the bottom curves up to the deck at both ends.
  9. It should leave a long red hull, a little wider at the top than at the bottom, made of a few pieces with small overlaps.

Tip: The hull sits on the water just below the shore line, toward the right edge; it's about three times as long as it is tall. Its left end comes to a point and its right end is blunter.

Building from pieces

Not checked yet

Motion. Start with one simple shape (an oval, a circle, or a rectangle). Then add the rest in curved pieces on each side, like ( ), smaller toward the edges.

What it leaves. A shape made of distinct curved segments with small gaps or overlaps between them.

Then. Soften where the pieces meet only if the picture shows smooth ribs; otherwise leave the segments visible.

STEP 8 OF 17 · The sailboat, 2 of 4

Paint the white sail

  1. Let the red hull, and the hill and the sea dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Rinse the brush well first. Dirty water tints every color with the last one.
  3. Optional: lightly chalk its outline first, from the transfer outline in Before you start, placed with the tape marks.
  4. Inside the outlined area. Its top is about 3 in from the top edge, and its right side is about 1 1/4 in from the right edge; it's about 3 in wide and 3 1/2 in tall.
  5. Paint: Warm white.
  6. Mix enough Warm white for this step and steps 9 and 14; cover it between them.
  7. Brush: 1/2 inch flat.
  8. Start with the bigger triangle just right of where the mast will go. Then add the narrower triangle on its left, the two meeting along the mast line.
  9. It should leave two white triangles side by side, with a thin gap or overlap where they meet.

Tip: The sail's tip is above the right end of the hull's middle; its bottom edge sits just above the deck. The right triangle is wider than the left. Leave a hairline gap down the middle where the mast will go.

STEP 9 OF 17 · The sailboat, 3 of 4

Line the deck rim

  1. Let the white sail and the red hull dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Inside the outlined area. Its bottom is about 4 in from the bottom edge, and its right side is about 1 in from the right edge; it's about 3 in wide and 1 in tall.
  3. Paint: Warm white.
  4. Brush: liner. Load: Thin the paint with water until it flows like ink: swirl the brush in water, then in the paint. Reload often.
  5. Hold the brush upright, with light, steady pressure, and pull one thin line along the top edge of the hull, from one end to the other.
  6. It should leave thin, flowing lines.
  7. Leave what step 7 painted showing around these marks, as in the Result picture.
  8. Warm white is much lighter than what it goes over: expect two or three thin coats, letting each dry.
  9. Watch out: Skippy, broken lines. The paint is too thick. Fix: add water.

Tip: Keep the line thin and level along the very top of the red; it separates the hull from the sail.

Liner work

Not checked yet

With. liner; small round (the tip)

Load. Thin the paint with water until it flows like ink: swirl the brush in water, then in the paint. Reload often.

Motion. Hold the brush upright, with light, steady pressure. For branches, start thick at the trunk and taper. Let branches fork in different directions and overlap, and wobble the edges a little.

What it leaves. Thin, flowing lines.

Then. Reload often.

Thin paint, upright brush

Dashed outline: what to paint in that picture. Arrows: which way to move the brush.

If it goes wrong.

  • Skippy, broken lines. The paint is too thick. Add water.
  • Lines spread or feather. The paint underneath is still wet. Only paint lines over dry paint.

Try a few lines on scrap paper first.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 10 OF 17 · The sailboat, 4 of 4

Paint the mast and boom

  1. Let the red hull and the white sail dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Rinse the brush well first. Dirty water tints every color with the last one.
  3. Inside the outlined area. Its top is about 2 1/2 in from the top edge, and its right side is about 1 in from the right edge; it's about 3 in wide and 4 in tall.
  4. Paints, darkest first: Dark plum-brown, then Mast brown. The paint map shows where each goes.
  5. Mix enough Dark plum-brown for this step and step 16; cover it between them.
  6. Brush: liner. Load: Thin the paint with water until it flows like ink: swirl the brush in water, then in the paint. Reload often.
  7. Hold the brush upright, with light, steady pressure. Pull the mast straight up from the deck to its tip in one stroke, then pull the boom across the bottom of the sail.
  8. It should leave thin, flowing lines.
  9. Watch out: Skippy, broken lines. The paint is too thick. Fix: add water.

Tip: The mast runs straight up between the two triangles of the sail and pokes a little above its tip; the boom runs along the sail's bottom edge. Use the darker paint for the mast's line and the lighter brown just along its edge.

How Claude read your photosubject, light, layers

Before starting

Subject: A red sailboat with a white sail on teal water at sunset, an orange sky going purple at the top, a low sun with its gold path on the water, and a purple hill on the left horizon.

Found in the image: just the picture

Done: none

Why: No bars, borders, captions, or frame around the painting.

Fitted to your canvas

Canvas: 14 x 11 in, landscape (11x14)

Done: crop

Left out: about 15% of the width: a strip of sky and water at the far left (the hill's left end) and at the far right.

Why: The photo is 3:2 and the canvas is 14:11; fit-canvas cropped about 7.5% off each side, keeping the boat, its reflection, the sun and its path whole.

Beginner version

What made it too busy: No tiny separate things beyond the subject (one boat), no texture of hundreds of items (the water ripples are one repeated mark: horizontal dashes), no detail inside big shapes beyond horizontal sky streaks, and about 8 parts (sky, sun, hill, far shore, water, sun path, boat, boat reflection), within the 8-part budget for a 154 sq in canvas.

Why: The picture is already a loose painterly scene a beginner can follow.

A calm sunset seascape: the small red-and-white sailboat right of center is the subject, set against a purple-to-orange sky with a low sun whose gold path runs down the teal water. What matters is the glowing sky blend, a clean boat silhouette, and water that reads as water (level strokes, reflections straight under their objects, ripples last). Hard parts for a beginner: white over orange needs coats, thin mast lines, and keeping reflections soft.

Subject: A small red sailboat with a white sail on calm teal water at sunset
Focal point: the white sail and red hull, right of center, with the low sun to their left
Light: the setting sun, low in the sky just left of center, behind the boat; light comes toward the viewer from the horizon

What it saw, back to front

  1. Sunset sky
  2. Hill and far shore
  3. The water
  4. The red hull
  5. The white sail
  6. Mast and boom
Why this techniquePaint along, back to front
ChosenPaint along, back to frontStart on a plain white canvas. Paint the sky first, then each part of the scene from farthest to nearest, each straight over the one behind it. Then the main subject, texture with simple brush moves, shadows, and highlights last.

Paint-along, back to front, is the owner's pick for beginner acrylic, and a sunset over water is a classic paint-along subject: sky, sun, far land, water, then the boat, then reflections and ripples.

Passed onBlock in, then build up

Tones the canvas and blocks in first; the owner's preferred beginner style is paint-along from a white canvas.

How the paint recipes were worked out14 paints, free

Paint doesn't mix like light on a screen: blue and yellow make green, not gray. So the recipes come from a pigment mixing model (Mixbox), not a guess. For each paint it tried every simple recipe from your tubes, up to three colors plus white, and kept the one that lands closest to the color in the painting. Delta E is how far off it lands: under 2 is hard to see, under 5 is close, and over 8 means these tubes can't quite make it.

Why the steps go in this order17 steps

Back to front: the sky first, run past the horizon; the sun on the dry sky; the hill and shore; the water base and its streaks; the boat (hull, sail, rim, mast) over the water; then, with everything above the water dry, the reflections in the research's order (sun path, boat reflection pulled down, zigzag mast) and the level ripple dashes last.

  1. 1. Blend the sunset sky

    The farthest thing, painted first and run past the horizon so the land and water go over it.

  2. 2. Paint the sun

    Sits on the sky, so it goes on once the sky is dry.

  3. 3. Paint the hill and far shore

    The next-farthest shape, over the dry sky.

  4. 4. Lay in the deep teal water

    The water's base coat, painted straight through where the boat and reflections go.

  5. 5. Work dark streaks into the water

    The water's darker and gray streaks, a pass over the dry base, so the texture builds instead of appearing at once.

  6. 6. Streak the mid teal across the water

    The lighter mid-teal streaks, a second texture pass (check said one pass turned too much flat to textured).

  7. 7. Block in the red hull

    The boat goes on over the dry water; the hull first as the base of the boat.

  8. 8. Paint the white sail

    White over the orange sky, after the hull so its foot sits on the deck.

  9. 9. Line the deck rim

    A thin light line over the dry hull, separating hull from sail.

  10. 10. Paint the mast and boom

    Liner lines last on the boat, over the dry sail.

  11. 11. Dash in the dull gold path

    Reflections go on once everything above the water is dry; the darker gold first.

  12. 12. Dash the bright gold on top

    The brighter gold over the middle, leaving the dull gold at the edges.

  13. 13. Pull down the sail's gray reflection

    The sail's reflection pulled straight down under the boat, its base value first.

  14. 14. Pull down the white of the sail

    The lighter streaks over the gray, broken by the water.

  15. 15. Pull down the red of the hull

    The hull's red reflection just under the hull.

  16. 16. Zigzag the mast's reflection

    The mast's reflection as a zigzag, after the colors it crosses.

  17. 17. Dash the light ripples

    Level ripple dashes last, crossing the reflections so they read as water.

What the reviewer caught7 notes

A second Claude, with fresh eyes and none of this reasoning, compared each picture with its neighbors and the finish. It gets two rounds of fixes, then stops; anything still off is flagged on its step. A third checked each step's words against a measured map of what the picture changed, asking whether a beginner following them would get there.

  • Finish check First finish (from the render cache): water a bright saturated turquoise-blue instead of the photo's muted teal, and the sky's soft streaks turned into blotchy cloud patches. Fixed by one redo.
  • Text check: drift Step 1: Faint ghosts of the sail (reddish triangle) and hull (teal patch) show in steps 1-6, and the hill and shore show faintly in step 1, before their own steps; 98_background.png rendered clean (no problems) but its colors inside the boat's outline differ from the finished sky and the steps paste it there. (left: the background render had no problems, so the skill allows no redo; the ghost is not an outline that's too tight)
  • Text check: drift Step 5: Steps 5-16 show a blurred gray-green smudge over the water where the sun path, streaks, ripples and reflection go, until each is painted. (left: no plan change removes it)
  • Text check: missing Step 8: A thin line shows where the mast goes before the mast step. (fixed)
  • Text check: missing Step 9: The hull's lower edge darkens in the rim step, with no paint for it. (left: no paint to give it a pass of its own)
  • Text check: wrong_result Step 11: The first sun path picture is a near-solid dull gold block, not dashes with water between. (left: the outline merges the dashes; the text asks for dashes)
  • Text check: missing Step 16: A dark band appears along the top of the reflection under the hull. (fixed)

What Claude would do differentlyfor the next lesson
  • Rewrote card lines for this subject: small-circles (cloud wording, on a sun), horizontal-strokes result ('ground or water') on land and water, build-from-pieces motion and result (oval and parentheses wording, on a hull and a sail), liner motion ('branches', on a deck rim and a mast), pull-down and zigzag results ('tree, boat, or shore'; 'mast, post, or plank').
  • draft-text listed the sky's paints 'top to bottom' as Sunset pink, Twilight purple, Sunset orange; the purple is at the top, so the line was rewritten.
  • draft-text said the sky 'reaches all four edges' though the sky step stops just below the horizon; rewritten.
  • The water needed two marks children (mid-teal streaks, light ripples) only to get under check's 10% flat-to-textured limit, because paints --add found no third distinct teal.
  • The streaks part's own paint merged into Deep teal (Delta E 9.1), so its step says to lighten Deep teal with a little white.
  • Not covered by the cards: no card for a deck rim line beyond liner work; no hull or sail stroke card (used build-from-pieces).
  • The first finish render came back from the render cache (cached: true), an identical call from an earlier run, and needed a redo for water and sky color.

Known problems

Where the pictures aren't quite right. Paint it the way the step says and use the picture as a guide.

  • Step 1, Blend the sunset sky: Faint ghosts of the sail (reddish triangle) and hull (teal patch) show in steps 1-6, and the hill and shore show faintly in step 1, before their own steps; 98_background.png rendered clean (no problems) but its colors inside the boat's outline differ from the finished sky and the steps paste it there.
  • Step 5, Work dark streaks into the water: Steps 5-16 show a blurred gray-green smudge over the water where the sun path, streaks, ripples and reflection go, until each is painted.
  • Step 9, Line the deck rim: The hull's lower edge darkens in the rim step, with no paint for it.
